desc:
You have n tasks; task i takes tasks[i] hours. You work in sessions of at most sessionTime consecutive hours each. A task must be finished entirely inside one session (it cannot be split between two sessions), and the tasks of a session may be done in any order.

Return the minimum number of sessions needed to complete all tasks. For example, tasks = [3, 1, 3, 1, 1] with sessionTime = 8 needs 2 sessions (3 + 1 + 3 + 1 and 1).
hints: Assign each task to a session. A new session is only needed when no existing session has enough room.
Backtrack over tasks one at a time: put the task in one of the sessions already opened (if it fits) or open a new one. Prune when the number of sessions opened is not better than the best found.

For a faster method, remember for every set of finished tasks (a bitmask) the best pair (sessions used, hours used in the last session). Adding a task either fits in the last session or starts a new one.
editorial: A simple backtracking solution places the tasks one by one. For task i, try every opened session where it fits, or open a new session; stop a branch when the number of sessions is at least the best found. Sorting tasks in decreasing order and skipping sessions with equal remaining room make it quick for small n.

A reliable O(2n · n) solution uses a bitmask table. Let dp[mask] be the lexicographically smallest pair (sessions, hours used in the last session) to complete the tasks in mask. From dp[mask], adding task i gives (s, l + t) if l + t ≤ sessionTime, otherwise (s + 1, t). Comparing pairs lexicographically is valid because fewer sessions always beats more, and with equal sessions a less filled last session leaves more room for later tasks. The answer is the first component of dp[all].
With n ≤ 14 the table has at most 16,384 states and about 230,000 transitions.
